questions.question: Where do business rules execute in the ServiceNow architecture?

options.text: In the user's web browser (client-side)
On the ServiceNow server (server-side)
In the MID Server
In the browser's service worker

explanation.correct: Business rules execute on the server side, not in the browser. They deal primarily with interaction with the database table itself. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Business rules run on the server, not the client. Client-side scripts such as Client Scripts and UI Policies run in the browser.
MID Servers are used for integrations and discovery, not for executing business rules.
Service workers are a browser technology unrelated to ServiceNow business rule execution.

source.excerpt: And these business rules execute on the server side, not in the browser. So they are faster, but they generally don't work on things like the form that you see in your browser or a list. They are dealing primarily with interaction with the table itself.

subtopics: Business rule types (before, after, async, display)

questions.question: Which of the following are types of business rules based on when they execute in the transaction lifecycle? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Before
After
Concurrent
Async

explanation.correct: ServiceNow business rules can be configured as before, after, display, before query, or async (asynchronous) types. Before, After, and Async are all valid business rule execution types. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: There is no 'Concurrent' business rule type in ServiceNow. The valid types are before, after, async, display, and before query.

source.excerpt: before rules, before we do something like a database update. After rules. After we have done a database update. And lastly, asynchronous rules are where it is not tied to the user's UI that's executing this.

subtopics: Business rule types (before, after, async, display)

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an asynchronous business rule?

options.text: To execute before a record is displayed to the user
To run non-time-sensitive logic without blocking the user's session
To validate field values before a record is saved to the database
To pass server-side data to client-side scripts using g_scratchpad

explanation.correct: Asynchronous business rules are used for operations that are not time-sensitive. They are added to the job queue and execute at the next available moment, returning control to the user's UI immediately. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Executing before a record is displayed describes a display business rule, not an asynchronous one.
Validating field values before saving describes a before business rule. Async rules run after the database operation and are queued as scheduled jobs.
Passing data to the client side via g_scratchpad is a feature of display business rules, not asynchronous rules.

source.excerpt: If something is not time sensitive and we don't want our user to be waiting around to get control of their resources again, their UI, we can create something as an asynchronous rule. Means it gets added to our job queue, and it executes when the next available spot is there.

subtopics: Business rule types (before, after, async, display)

questions.question: Which type of business rule supports the use of g_scratchpad to pass data from the server to the client?

options.text: Before business rule
After business rule
Display business rule
Async business rule

explanation.correct: The g_scratchpad object is only available in display business rules. It provides a mechanism to pass server-side data to client-side scripts. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/reference/r_DisplayBusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Before business rules execute before a database operation and do not have access to g_scratchpad. They use the current and previous objects for field manipulation.
After business rules execute after the database operation completes. They do not support g_scratchpad for passing data to the client.
Async business rules run as scheduled jobs separate from the user's session and have no mechanism to pass data to the client UI.

source.excerpt: we have this thing called g_scratchpad, which only works with display business rules. And it allows us to take data from the server side and pass it to the client side.

subtopics: Business rule types (before, after, async, display)

questions.question: A developer needs to automatically populate a calculated field value on an Incident record before it is written to the database, without the user explicitly setting it. Which type of business rule should the developer use?

options.text: Display business rule
Before business rule
After business rule
Async business rule

explanation.correct: A before business rule runs after the form is submitted but before the record is written to the database, making it ideal for populating or modifying field values before the save occurs. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Display business rules run when a record is read and before it is displayed. They are used for passing data to the client via g_scratchpad, not for modifying field values before a save.
After business rules run after the record is already saved to the database, so they cannot populate field values before the write occurs.
Async business rules are queued as scheduled jobs and run independently of the current transaction, making them unsuitable for modifying field values before a record is saved.

source.excerpt: Before we do a record update. So maybe we have submitted the record, but before it actually gets written to the database, we're going to execute this rule. Maybe we need to populate fields that are not populated by the user. Populate a field in that record.

subtopics: Business rule types (before, after, async, display)
When to use business rules vs other methods

questions.question: Why are the current and previous objects NOT available in scheduled script executions?

options.text: Scheduled scripts run on the client side where these objects are not supported
Scheduled scripts are not associated with a specific table record
Scheduled scripts only support GlideForm (g_form) APIs
The current and previous objects are deprecated in the Yokohama release

explanation.correct: The current and previous objects are only available in server-side scripts that are associated with a specific table record (i.e., scripts with a table field on the trigger). Scheduled scripts have no table association, so GlideRecord or GlideQuery must be used instead. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/server-scripting/concept/c_ScheduledJobs.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Scheduled scripts run on the server side, not the client side. The reason current/previous are unavailable is the lack of a table record context, not the execution environment.
GlideForm (g_form) is a client-side API and is not available in scheduled scripts. Scheduled scripts use server-side APIs like GlideRecord and GlideQuery.
The current and previous objects are not deprecated. They remain fully supported in business rules and other table-associated server-side scripts.

source.excerpt: we cannot use the current or previous object... Generally speaking, the current and previous objects are only available in server-side script that are associated with a specific table record. And that means, generally, that there is a table field on the trigger. No table field on this trigger.

questions.question: A developer writes the expression current.caller_id.department.name in a business rule on the Incident table. What technique is being used and what value is returned?

options.text: Dot-walking — returns the name of the department of the caller on the incident
GlideRecord chaining — returns the sys_id of the caller's department
Reference querying — returns the caller's user name
Object inheritance — returns the incident's department field

explanation.correct: This is dot-walking, which traverses reference fields across tables. Starting from the current Incident record, it follows caller_id to the User table, then department to the Department table, and retrieves the Name field value. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/server-scripting/concept/c_DotWalkingInScripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: This is dot-walking, not GlideRecord chaining. Dot-walking resolves the display value (the name), not the sys_id, when accessing the .name field.
The expression navigates to the department's name, not the caller's user name. Reference querying is not a ServiceNow term for this technique.
Object inheritance is a general programming concept unrelated to traversing reference fields in ServiceNow. The expression returns the caller's department name, not a field on the incident itself.

source.excerpt: current.caller_id.department.name is going to give us sales because that's what that callers department's name is. And we're going from table to table to table. This is Dot-walking.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid database operations that can trigger a business rule in ServiceNow? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Insert
Update
Export
Delete

explanation.correct: Business rules can be triggered on insert, update, delete, and query operations against a table. Export is not a database operation that triggers business rules. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Export is a UI/reporting operation, not a database operation. Business rules are triggered by database-level operations such as insert, update, delete, and query.

source.excerpt: business rule is a record that we create that contains JavaScript to do something related to a table. We want to display a record, we want to insert a record, update a record, or delete a record, or just query the table. We can run the business rule when any of these things happen.

questions.question: In an onChange client script, what does the 'oldValue' parameter represent?

options.text: The value of the field immediately before the most recent user edit on the client side
The value stored on the server when the form was loaded
The default value defined in the field's dictionary entry
The value from the same field on the previously viewed record

explanation.correct: The oldValue parameter in an onChange client script represents the value that was stored on the server when the form loaded. It does not track intermediate client-side edits — if a user changes the field 20 times before saving, oldValue still reflects the original server-side value. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/client-scripts/concept/c_ClientScripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: oldValue does not track each intermediate client-side change. It specifically reflects the server-side stored value at form load time, regardless of how many times the field has been edited in the current session.

oldValue is not the dictionary default value. It is the actual value stored in the database when the form loaded. For a new record, oldValue would be null or blank, which may coincide with a default but is not derived from the dictionary definition.
oldValue has no relation to previously viewed records. It is scoped to the current record and form session, representing only the server-side stored value at load time.

source.excerpt: Know that 'oldValue' is equivalent to the previous value when the form loaded, not what was previously there if you've edited the field 20 times before saving it, but rather, you can think of it as what's stored there on the server.

subtopics: When to use business rules vs other methods

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Execute if false' script section in a UI policy?

options.text: It runs validation logic before the UI policy condition is evaluated
It defines scripted actions to perform when the UI policy condition is no longer true
It prevents the UI policy from executing on specific form views
It logs diagnostic information when the UI policy condition fails to evaluate

explanation.correct: The 'Execute if false' script section in a UI policy allows developers to define actions that should occur when the UI policy condition evaluates to false (i.e., is no longer met). This is essential for undoing scripted changes such as clearing field messages when the triggering condition changes. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/client_scripting/client-side_policies/concept/c_UIPolicies.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The 'Execute if false' script does not run validation before condition evaluation. It is triggered after the condition is evaluated and found to be false, allowing the developer to reverse previously applied scripted changes.

Restricting a UI policy to specific form views is controlled by the View field on the UI policy record, not the 'Execute if false' script. The script is exclusively for defining reversal logic when the condition is no longer met.

The 'Execute if false' script does not provide logging or diagnostic capabilities. It is a scripting area for defining what should happen when the UI policy condition evaluates to false, such as removing field messages or resetting styles.

source.excerpt: That's what the execute if false field is for. And, remember, during my lecture, I said that, at least at present, despite all the advances in Now Assist and GenAI and stuff like that, ServiceNow can't parse this and figure out the opposite of what you intended it to do and then just do that.

questions.question: A developer creates a scripted UI policy that uses g_form.showFieldMessage() to display an informational message beneath a field when a condition is met. After testing, the developer notices the message remains visible even after the condition is no longer true. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The showFieldMessage() method requires a form save before it can be cleared
The developer did not add a corresponding script in the 'Execute if false' section to clear the message
UI policy scripts cannot interact with field messages and a client script should be used instead
The UI policy's 'Reverse if false' checkbox is not selected on the UI policy record

explanation.correct: When a UI policy uses scripting (such as g_form.showFieldMessage()) to modify the form, the platform cannot automatically reverse those scripted changes when the condition becomes false. The developer must explicitly add reversal logic in the 'Execute if false' script section — for example, calling g_form.hideFieldMessage() to remove the message. UI policy actions auto-reverse, but scripts do not. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/client_scripting/client-side_policies/concept/c_UIPolicies.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: g_form.showFieldMessage() is a client-side method that takes effect immediately without a form save. Clearing the message also does not require saving — it requires the corresponding clearance logic in the 'Execute if false' script.
UI policy scripts can absolutely interact with field messages using GlideForm methods like showFieldMessage() and hideFieldMessage(). This is a common and supported pattern for scripted UI policies.

'Reverse if false' applies to UI policy action records (such as making a field read-only or mandatory), not to scripted behavior. Scripted actions in the 'Execute if true' section must be manually reversed in the 'Execute if false' section.

source.excerpt: I told it indeed to create this message every time the condition became true. But I never told it to undo the message. That's what the execute if false field is for.

questions.question: Which of the following are parameters provided by the onChange client script template function? (Select all that apply)

options.text: control
current
isLoading
previous

explanation.correct: The onChange client script template function provides five parameters: control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading, and isTemplate. The 'control' parameter gives access to the UI element of the field, while 'isLoading' is a boolean indicating whether the form is still loading. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/script/client-scripts/concept/c_ClientScripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: 'current' is a server-side GlideRecord object available in business rules, not a client script parameter. In business rules, 'current' represents the record being inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. Client scripts use GlideForm (g_form) methods and the onChange template parameters instead.

'previous' is a server-side GlideRecord object available in business rules that contains the record values before the current update. It is not available in client scripts. The client-side equivalent for tracking value changes is the 'oldValue' parameter in the onChange template.

source.excerpt: I'm going to leverage a few of these values that are given to me as part of 'onChange' Template function. New value will let me grab whatever's currently in that field at any given time, and 'control' actually gives me access to that UI element of the field itself.

subtopics: When to use business rules vs other methods

questions.question: A developer needs to make a field read-only when a UI policy condition is true. The developer is deciding whether to use a UI policy action record or accomplish this entirely through scripting. What is a key advantage of using a UI policy action record for this requirement?

options.text: UI policy actions execute on the server side, providing better security than client-side scripts
UI policy actions automatically reverse the change when the condition is no longer met, without requiring additional scripting
UI policy actions support conditional logic that cannot be replicated in scripts
UI policy actions allow setting multiple field attributes in a single line of code

explanation.correct: UI policy action records are lightweight and automatically reverse their effects when the UI policy condition is no longer true. For example, if an action sets a field to read-only, the platform automatically makes it editable again when the condition becomes false — no additional scripting required. This auto-reversal is a key advantage over scripted approaches, which require explicit 'Execute if false' logic. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/client_scripting/client-side_policies/concept/c_UIPolicies.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policy actions are client-side configurations, not server-side. They control the form presentation in the user's browser. For server-side enforcement of field values, Access Control Rules (ACLs) or business rules would be used.

UI policy actions do not support conditional logic themselves — the condition is defined on the parent UI policy record. Scripts actually offer more flexibility for complex conditional logic than action records do.

UI policy actions are configured as separate records (one per field attribute change), not as single lines of code. Each action record controls one attribute (read-only, mandatory, or visible) for one field.

source.excerpt: UI policy action records are so lightweight and so clear, I can make it once and never worry about it... It can parse and figure out the opposite of this true value on the read-onlyness of our original CP field, as dictated in the UI policy action record.

subtopics: When to use business rules vs other methods

questions.question: A developer is writing an onChange client script that must replace the current value of a field with a corrected value and display an error message to the user when an invalid entry is detected. Which two GlideForm (g_form) methods should the developer use? (Select all that apply)

options.text: g_form.setValue()
g_form.setDisplay()
g_form.addErrorMessage()
g_form.setReadOnly()

explanation.correct: To programmatically replace a field value on the client side, the developer should use g_form.setValue() with the field name and new value as arguments. To display an error message banner at the top of the form, g_form.addErrorMessage() is the appropriate method. These two methods together fulfill the requirements of replacing the invalid value and notifying the user. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/yokohama-application-development/page/app-store/dev_portal/API_reference/GlideForm/concept/c_GlideFormAPI.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: g_form.setDisplay() controls whether a field is visible or hidden on the form. It does not replace field values or display error messages. It is used for showing/hiding fields based on conditions.

g_form.setReadOnly() makes a field read-only or editable. While this might be used as an additional step to prevent further editing, it does not replace the field value or display an error message, which are the two specific requirements stated.

source.excerpt: When we set values client-side, we usually have to use a GlideForm method-- I bet you know this-- called 'setValue.' And in this case, I'm going to call out the field name explicitly using its system name.

questions.question: A developer needs to pass server-side data to a client script without using an AJAX call. Which type of business rule and mechanism should they use?

options.text: Before business rule with current object
Display business rule with g_scratchpad
After business rule with gs.addInfoMessage()
Async business rule with GlideAjax

explanation.correct: Display business rules run when a form is loaded (before display) and can use g_scratchpad to pass server-side data to client scripts. g_scratchpad is only available in display business rules. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_DisplayBusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Before business rules execute before a database operation (insert/update/delete) and cannot pass data to client scripts via g_scratchpad.
While gs.addInfoMessage() displays a message on the form, it does not provide structured data access for client scripts to consume.
Async business rules run as scheduled jobs after the transaction completes and have no connection to the client-side UI.

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: we have this thing called g_scratchpad, which only works with display business rules. And it allows us to take data from the server side and pass it to the client side.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid GlideSystem logging methods that write to the system log? (Choose two.)

options.text: gs.info()
gs.print()
gs.warn()
gs.console()

explanation.correct: gs.info() logs informational messages and gs.warn() logs warning messages to the system log (syslog). Other valid methods include gs.error(), gs.debug(), and gs.log(). See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/server-scripting/concept/c_GlideSystemLogging.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: gs.print() is used to write to the screen/output in background scripts, not to the system log table.
gs.console() does not exist as a GlideSystem method. Console logging is a browser-side concept (console.log).

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: gs.info, for informational events; error, for critical errors; warn, for things that might be an issue; debug, just when we're in debug mode

questions.question: A developer has a business rule that sends email notifications after an incident is created. Users report that form submissions are slow. What change would improve performance?

options.text: Change the business rule from 'after' to 'before'
Change the business rule to 'async' (asynchronous)
Change the business rule to 'display'
Add the Advanced checkbox and rewrite in JavaScript

explanation.correct: Asynchronous business rules run as scheduled jobs separate from the user's transaction, so the user regains control of their UI immediately. Email notifications are not time-sensitive enough to block the user's session. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_AsyncBusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Before business rules still execute synchronously within the user's transaction. They run before the database write but still block the UI.
Display business rules run when a form is loaded for viewing, not when records are created or updated. They cannot send notifications on insert.
The business rule is already using JavaScript. The Advanced checkbox just reveals the script editor. The issue is timing (sync vs async), not the scripting approach.

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: When possible, use asynchronous business rules. And we do this so that the user is not waiting on this script to execute before they can continue anything else.

questions.question: Which statement about the Script Debugger for business rules is correct?

options.text: Breakpoints set by one developer are visible to all other developers
Asynchronous business rules can be stepped through in the Script Debugger
Each developer's debug session is independent with their own breakpoints
The Script Debugger modifies the production script during debugging

explanation.correct: The Script Debugger creates a unique session per developer. Breakpoints are session-specific and not shared with or visible to other developers. Multiple developers can debug the same script simultaneously without interfering. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/server-scripting/concept/c_ScriptDebugger.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Breakpoints are session-specific. Each developer's breakpoints are private and not visible to others.
Asynchronous business rules become scheduled jobs and cannot be stepped through in the Script Debugger because they don't execute within the interactive session.
The Script Debugger only reads and pauses the script during execution. It does not modify the saved script code.

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: each developer, anytime they open up the Script Debugger, it is its own session. The breakpoints you set are specific to that session. They are not global

questions.question: In a 'before' business rule, what is unique about modifying the current record compared to an 'after' business rule?

options.text: Before rules require an explicit current.update() call to save changes
Before rules can modify the current record without calling update() because the record hasn't been written yet
Before rules cannot access the current object at all
Before rules automatically create a new version of the record

explanation.correct: In a 'before' business rule, changes to the current object are automatically included when the record is written to the database, since the write hasn't happened yet. In contrast, 'after' business rules require explicit update() calls because the record has already been saved. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/business-rules/concept/c_BusinessRules.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Calling current.update() in a before rule is actually an anti-pattern that can cause recursive execution. The changes are saved automatically with the pending write.
Before business rules have full access to the current object. They can read and modify field values before the database write occurs.
Business rules do not create record versions. Version tracking is handled by auditing configuration, not business rule types.

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: before we do a record update... the records been submitted... before it's actually written to the database, we are going to execute a rule to perform some activity

questions.question: A developer needs to access the department name of the caller on an incident record in a business rule. Which Dot-walking expression is correct?

options.text: current.caller_id.getDepartment().name
current.caller_id.department.name
current.department.caller_id.name
gs.getUser().department.name

explanation.correct: Dot-walking allows traversal from the current record through reference fields to related tables. current.caller_id references the User table, .department references the Department table from the user, and .name gets the department's name. See: https://docs.servicenow.com/bundle/xanadu-application-development/page/script/server-scripting/concept/c_DotWalkingInScripts.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: getDepartment() is not a GlideRecord method. Dot-walking uses field names directly, not getter methods for reference traversal.
This reverses the relationship. The incident table doesn't have a department field directly; department is on the user (caller_id) record.
gs.getUser() returns the currently logged-in user, not the caller on the incident. This would get the wrong user's department.

references: Scripting in ServiceNow Fundamentals - Business Rules

source.excerpt: current.caller_id.department.name is going to give us sales because that's what that callers department's name is. And we're going from table to table to table. This is Dot-walking.

questions.question: A business rule is configured to run 'before' insert on the Incident table. The rule sets a value on the 'description' field. A developer notices the value is not being saved. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The business rule should use current.update() to save the change
Another business rule running 'after' is overwriting the value
The business rule order number is too high, causing it to run after the record is saved
A client script is overwriting the value after the form reloads

explanation.correct: If a client script sets the description field when the form loads, it will overwrite the value set by the before business rule. The record saves correctly but the client script changes the display.

wrongAnswers.explanation: In a 'before' business rule, you should NOT call current.update(). Changes to current are automatically saved when the before rule completes.
An 'after' business rule cannot overwrite a value set in a 'before' rule unless it explicitly calls current.update(), which is not standard practice.
The order number determines the sequence among business rules of the same timing (before/after), not when they run relative to the database operation.

questions.question: Which THREE of the following are valid business rule timing options in ServiceNow? (Choose 3)

options.text: before
during
after
async
display

explanation.correct: ServiceNow business rules support four timing options: before, after, async, and display. Before runs before the database operation, after runs immediately after, and display runs when a form is loaded.

wrongAnswers.explanation: 'During' is not a valid business rule timing option in ServiceNow.
Async is actually a valid timing option — business rules can run asynchronously. However, the question asks for three, and before, after, and display are the three most fundamental timing options.

questions.question: A developer needs to prevent a record from being deleted if it has associated child records. Which business rule configuration should they use?

options.text: Before delete business rule that calls current.setAbortAction(true)
After delete business rule that restores the record
Before delete business rule that calls current.deleteRecord()
Display business rule that hides the delete button

explanation.correct: A before delete business rule with current.setAbortAction(true) prevents the delete operation from proceeding. This is the standard pattern for preventing deletions based on conditions.

wrongAnswers.explanation: An after delete business rule runs after the record is already deleted. You cannot reliably restore a deleted record this way.
Calling deleteRecord() in a before delete rule would cause recursion and does not prevent the deletion.
Hiding the delete button through a display business rule is a UI-only approach. Users could still delete via list actions, APIs, or other means.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'current.operation()' method in a business rule?

options.text: Returns the name of the current business rule
Returns the database operation being performed (insert, update, delete, query)
Returns the execution order of the current rule
Returns the table name the business rule is running on

explanation.correct: current.operation() returns the current database operation: insert, update, delete, or query. This is useful in business rules that run on multiple operations.

wrongAnswers.explanation: To get the business rule name, you would check the business rule record, not use current.operation().
The execution order is determined by the Order field on the business rule record, not by current.operation().
To get the table name, use current.getTableName(), not current.operation().
